Before the exact definitions, notice how often these two words get used as if they mean the same thing.
One of these asks where the bytes are. The other asks who can be legally forced to produce them, no matter where that is. Which is which?
answer: Sovereignty is the compelled-access question — the US CLOUD Act's own reach is the textbook case.
Residency only ever answers location. Sovereignty answers something completely different: who can be made to hand the data over, regardless of where it physically sits.

Where the bytes rest. Who can compel them. Whether a law requires that location in the first place. Blur these together, and you've made the mistake this whole topic exists to prevent.

The statute's own words say the disclosure obligation applies regardless of where the data sits. Possession and control are the test — not geography.

If you only remember one line: three separate questions, one framework whose status keeps shifting, and every mitigation with a limit worth saying out loud.
Residency, sovereignty, localisation. The CLOUD Act's possession test. A framework under appeal. And a key that protects everything, until the processing itself needs to see it.
Before I answer, notice what's already true in this scenario: the storage never left the EU, and no law required it to be anywhere else.
So residency and localisation are both already fine here. What's the actual question this scenario is testing?
answer: Whether the remote viewing session itself counts as a transfer.

Residency and localisation were never the exposure here — they're both satisfied. The real question is whether someone outside the EU looking at the data, even without moving it, is itself a transfer.
